http://www.euronews.com/2026/08/12/more-.text: Over 16,000 civilians captured by Russia during its conflict in Ukraine are still "deprived of their liberty," with many being held incommunicado and for reasons that violate international law, an informal UN security council meeting has been told.According to Claudia Fuentes Julio, the UN assistant secretary-general for human rights. “Widespread and systematic torture and ill-treatment” of both Ukrainian civilian detainees and prisoners of war by Russia are continuing, including sexual violence.Julio gave the estimates at the informal meeting of the Security Council called by Latvia and the United Kingdom on Monday to spotlight the plight of civilians and soldiers taken during the war that Russia launched with a full-scale invasion of its neighbor in February 2022.The council, which counts Russia as a permanent member, heard the accounts as both Russia and Ukraine have escalated attacks in the four-year conflict.According to Julio, since the invasion, 910 Ukrainian prisoners of war and 403 civilian detainees have been interviewed by UN human rights personnel following their release.And more than 95% of the Ukrainian prisoners of war and 85% of the civilian detainees reported being tortured or ill-treated, often repeatedly, the U.N. official said.They also reported sexual attacks and inhumane conditions, including food deprivation and inadequate medical services.The Geneva-based human rights office “has documented the execution of 129 Ukrainian prisoners of war at the beginning of their captivity and the deaths of 48 Ukrainian prisoners of war in custody, resulting from torture, denial of medical care, or other inhumane conditions of detention,” Julio said.The UN has not been permitted to visit Russian detention facilities, and its estimate of the number of people detained does not include a breakdown of adults and children.Some former detainees shared their ordeal with the UNThe Security Council also heard emotionally wrenching accounts from some former detainees who shared their ordeal.Crimean Tatar human rights activist Leniie Umerova, who called herself a “political prisoner” of the Russians for almost two years, and Khuan Leyva Garsiya, a Ukrainian soldier who was among the hundreds that held out for months at the Azovstal steel plant in the besieged city of Mariupol before turning themselves over to the Russians in May 2022 shared their stories.Garsiya, who was born in Mariupol to a Ukrainian mother and Cuban father, spent 1,183 days as a POW. He said he weighed 55 kilograms (120 pounds) when he was freed, pulling out a picture of his emaciated body to show the council.Garsiya said he was tortured, beaten harder, and humiliated more than other prisoners because the Russians suspected that he was a foreign mercenary due to his Cuban ancestry or an American spy because he went to college in the United States.“Russians were outraged that someone with a connection to Cuba, whom they consider an ally, would fight against their occupation army,” said Garsiya, who is still in the Ukrainian military.UN also said Russian detainees reported abusesUN human rights experts also interviewed 816 Russians and 57 third-country national prisoners of war from over 45 countries who were members of the Russian armed forces in Ukraine, said Julio, the assistant secretary-general.About half reported torture or ill-treatment, primarily during the initial stages of captivity and interrogation by Ukrainians, she said.But UN monitors reported that once they arrived in Ukrainian detention facilities, “the conditions generally comply with international humanitarian law and have improved since 2022.”Responding to the claims, Russia’s deputy UN Ambassador Maria Zabolotskaya told the council the Russian armed forces are complying with international humanitarian law, which includes the treatment of prisoners. She claimed Russian prisoners in Ukraine faced “torture and degradation and moral and physical abuse.”She called the Security Council meeting part of “a disinformation campaign against Russia,” funded by NATO countries involved in the Ukraine conflict. The aim, she said, “is to derail efforts towards a peace settlement and to justify strikes on the territory of Russia and against civilians.”For Ukraine's part, Volodymyr Pavlichenko, Kyiv's deputy UN ambassador, expressed his displeasure that Russia was not prepared to talk about the return of POWs, "including their POWs," and all civilian detainees, including kidnaped children.

https://www.politico.eu/article/russia-g.text: The German consulate in St. Petersburg must close by Sept. 18, in response to Berlin’s recent “unfriendly actions,” Russia’s foreign ministry announced Monday. While the embassy and consular services in Moscow remain open, the consulate in the northwest of the country must cease all operations and all staff must leave Russia by the specified date. “It was the German authorities that once again provoked a new round of escalation in bilateral relations. All responsibility for the consequences lies entirely with the Government of Germany,” the statement reads, referring to Berlin’s announcement last week that Russia was behind a drone attack on German territory. Advertisement Advertisement The attempted attack involved three drones carrying explosive material spotted at or near the Leipzig-Halle Airport, one of which was found near a Ukrainian Antonov plane used to transport munitions . Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul unveiled a series of domestic countermeasures against the Kremlin, including the closure on Sept. 18 of Russia’s consulate in Bonn and the Russian House cultural institution in Berlin. Russia also said it would close branches of the German cultural center, the Goethe-Institut, in Moscow, Saint Petersburg, and Novosibirsk. In recent months, EU countries have faced a growing number of suspected Russian attacks targeting military and critical infrastructure. In August, two drones were spotted over a Bundeswehr site in Germany, while Poland investigated the deliberate arson of a drone factory near Warsaw as possible foreign sabotage. Interior Minister Alexander Dorbindt warned that his country has yet to witness more attacks: “We assume that Germany is the target of further hybrid attacks by Russia. It can also be assumed that there is a willingness to cause even greater damage through hybrid attacks,” he said .

https://www.politico.eu/article/eu-lawma.text: BRUSSELS — New powers proposed for the EU's border police Frontex to monitor social media pose a threat to free speech, European lawmakers and civil society groups have told POLITICO. The EU Commission's proposal Tuesday for a major revamp of the coast and border patrol agency included a broad and explicit mandate to monitor social media for information that aids or encourages illegal border crossings into the European Union. Social democratic Italian lawmaker Brando Benifei told POLITICO it was "legitimate" for authorities to remove online advertisements for human smuggling: "But a broad social media surveillance mandate goes much further, placing online speech under a border agency’s watch.” Advertisement Advertisement After a 2019 monitoring tender with similar powers was revoked over criticism about privacy violations, Benifei said "the Commission now proposes copying ICE’s invasive online tracking,” referencing the much-criticized surveillance tactics of the U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agency. Under the EU proposal, Frontex would set up an internal structure to monitor social media and report to the platform in question the content it says is facilitating illegal entry to EU countries. This comes as the Commission is seeking to double the agency's budget for the next seven years and vastly expand its powers to deport people. The EU already has several structures that facilitate the exchange of information between civil society, social media platforms and authorities when it comes to disinformation campaigns or illegal content. These include a rapid response system on disinformation campaigns under the Digital Services Act (DSA), the EU's landmark law regulating digital platforms, as well as a recently established democratic resilience center. Policing content Brussels must tread a careful balance not to police individual pieces of content, especially given criticism from civil society activists that it is trying to become the arbiter of truth online. The legality of content is set by countries, which assign their authorities or civil society to monitor the platforms for problematic postings to be flagged to the platforms to be taken down. Frontex would apply for trusted flagger status under the DSA, which gives priority to the content it flags to social media platforms. Entities that apply for this status have to demonstrate expertise and independence to a national authority, which grants them special status. “The DSA’s trusted flagger program was never conceived for police forces to circumvent due process when assessing the legality of people’s online expression,” said Jan Penfrat, senior policy advisor at civil society group EDRi. Advertisement Advertisement The Commission's initial communication suggested Frontex "will be acting" as such an entity, which EU tech chief Henna Virkkunen later clarified meant they would apply for it. That application would have to be reviewed by a national authority to check Frontex's independence and expertise in that area. Polish right-wing MEP Piotr Müller told POLITICO that the "mandate must be precise" in focusing on criminal networks. “Frontex should go after smugglers and human traffickers, not police opinions about migration.” Müller is among those that criticize the DSA as policing free speech online. Executive Vice President Virkkunen announced the news at a meeting Tuesday of signatories of the DSA’s code of conduct on disinformation, some of whom are trusted flaggers. Questions around the implications of the measures for freedom of speech and assembly came up in the closed-door meeting. According to two attendees, Renate Nikolay, deputy director general of DG CONNECT, the Commission's tech department, tried to assuage the free-speech concerns. Other lawmakers took a positive, yet reserved, stance towards the changes in Frontex's mandate. The EU's migration authorities "need the tools to respond to the changing threats at Europe’s borders, including smugglers using social media to spread lies and promote dangerous crossings," which can include "better monitoring and information-sharing," Regina Doherty, a center-right MEP from Ireland told POLITICO. But "the priority now is to get the detail right so authorities can act quickly within a clear legal framework, and platforms take responsibility for illegal content," she pointed out. Austrian center-right MEP Andreas Schwab said that “social media clearly is becoming more and more a concern, but we should not have too many tools – let’s make use of the DSA.” Advertisement Advertisement Another MEP who knows the agency well was more blunt. Fabrice Leggeri, a former director of Frontex who hails from the far-right French National Rally party, said that the new powers amounted to an “attempt to censor freedom of speech in Europe” by Commission President Ursula Von der Leyen. The Commission didn't respond to POLITICO's repeated requests for comment on Frontex's expertise in this domain. Max Griera contributed to this report.
